passages.title: Interview with a young swimmer
passages.text:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Lucy Grant, who has just been chosen for the national swimming team at the age of seventeen. Lucy, when did you first start swimming?
Lucy: I was seven. Everyone assumes I loved it from the very beginning, but actually I was terrified of putting my face in the water. My older brother was the keen one. I only went along because Mum didn't want to drive to the pool twice. The lessons themselves were fun, though. Our teacher turned everything into a game.

Interviewer: Now you train at five o'clock in the morning. That must be hard.
Lucy: People always say that's the worst part. And at first I hated hearing the alarm. But now I actually love it. The pool's really quiet, and I feel I've already achieved something before the day starts. My teachers used to ask if I fell asleep in class, but I'm more awake than anyone! What I find harder is the evenings, when my friends go out and I have to be in bed by nine.

Interviewer: You changed coaches two years ago. Why was that?
Lucy: My first coach was lovely, and she had loads of experience. The club was just round the corner from my house, too. But she mainly worked with sprinters, and I'd started to realise that I was better at longer races, like the eight hundred metres. So I joined a club that specialises in distance swimming. It means a longer journey, but it was the right decision.

Interviewer: Last year you didn't make the final at the national championships. How did you deal with that?
Lucy: Of course I was disappointed for a day or two. Some people said I'd been unlucky, because I had a cold that week, but that wasn't really it. When my coach and I watched the video, it was obvious that my starts were too slow. So we worked on them all winter. Looking back, it was the best thing that could have happened, because I'm much faster now.

Interviewer: You're quite popular on social media. How do you feel about that side of things?
Lucy: Some swimmers say it adds a lot of pressure, but I don't feel that at all. And I only post once a week, so it doesn't take up much time. The best thing is when girls send me messages saying they've joined a swimming club because they watched my videos. That makes it all worth it.

Interviewer: Finally, what advice would you give to young swimmers?
Lucy: Don't worry about finding the perfect club or buying expensive kit. And please don't compare yourself with other swimmers all the time. The most important thing is to make sure you're having fun. If you aren't enjoying it, you won't keep going when it gets difficult.
Interviewer: Lucy Grant, thank you very much.

questions.question: How did Lucy feel when she first started swimming?
options: a) Bored by the lessons at the pool
b) Excited to be doing the same sport as her brother
c) Frightened of one part of swimming
questions.explanation: Lucy says "I was terrified of putting my face in the water." It was her brother who was keen, not her, and the lessons "were fun" because the teacher turned everything into a game.

questions.question: What does Lucy say about training early in the morning?
options: a) She has come to enjoy it.
b) It is the hardest part of her routine.
c) It makes her feel tired at school.
questions.explanation: She hated the alarm at first, "But now I actually love it." She says the evenings are harder, and at school she is "more awake than anyone".

questions.question: Why did Lucy change coaches?
options: a) She wanted to focus on a different kind of race.
b) Her first coach did not have enough experience.
c) Her first club was too far from her home.
questions.explanation: Her first coach "mainly worked with sprinters", but Lucy realised she "was better at longer races", so she joined a club that specialises in distance swimming. The coach "had loads of experience" and the old club was "just round the corner".

questions.question: How does Lucy feel now about her result at last year's national championships?
options: a) She believes she was unlucky.
b) She is still annoyed with herself about it.
c) She thinks it helped her to improve.
questions.explanation: She says "it was the best thing that could have happened, because I'm much faster now", after working on her slow starts. She was only disappointed "for a day or two", and she rejects the idea that she was unlucky: "that wasn't really it".

questions.question: What is Lucy's opinion of using social media?
options: a) It puts too much pressure on young athletes.
b) It is a good way to encourage other people.
c) It takes up too much of her time.
questions.explanation: The best thing for her is when girls join a swimming club "because they watched my videos" - "That makes it all worth it." She only posts once a week, so it "doesn't take up much time", and although some swimmers talk about pressure, she says "I don't feel that at all".

questions.question: What advice does Lucy give to young swimmers?
options: a) Check your progress against other swimmers.
b) Make sure you enjoy what you are doing.
c) Look for the best club you can find.
questions.explanation: She says "The most important thing is to make sure you're having fun." She tells them not to worry about "finding the perfect club" and not to "compare yourself with other swimmers all the time".
